 News Raise personal tax allowance to £20,000 update as Saturday deadline to act
 Chancellor John Healey is being told the frozen HMRC income tax threshold needs to rise from £12,570
 walesonline Bookmark 
 Share 
 Comments 
 News By Ben Hurst 09:07, 8 NOV 2026 
 Bookmark 
 Chancellor John Healey is being urged to raise the lowest income tax threshold (Image: Getty Images) Get the latest Cambridgeshire Live breaking news on WhatsApp
 Our community members are treated to special offers, promotions and adverts from us and our partners. You can check out at any time. More info 
 Join us on WhatsApp Members of the public have just six days left to put pressure on the Andy Burnham government over frozen tax thresholds. In last month's budget, Chancellor John Healey declined to make any changes despite widespread calls to do so.
 A petition on the Parliament website is calling for the lowest level of tax — currently set at £12,570 — to be raised to £20,000.
 The deadline to sign is Saturday, 14th November, and should it reach 10,000 signatures, the Treasury will be obliged to respond and set out its position on any potential changes.
 Income tax thresholds have remained frozen since 2021 and, under existing plans, will continue to do so until 2031.
 As a result, some of the lowest-paid workers are being drawn into paying ever-increasing amounts of tax — a phenomenon widely referred to as 'fiscal drag'. The basic Personal Allowance in the UK stands at £12,570 for the 2026/27 tax year, representing the amount you can earn annually before being liable for 20 per cent income tax.
 The higher 40% rate applies from £50,271, while the additional 45% rate kicks in at £125,140. Independent figures suggest that a basic-rate earner (£20k-£50k) is paying roughly £700 to £800 more in tax each year solely as a consequence of the freeze.
 The petition, created by Wade Reid, states: "The personal allowance has been frozen while living costs have risen, meaning workers pay more tax in real terms. Increasing it to £20,000 would put more money into millions of workers' pockets, helping with rising bills and supporting low and middle earners.
 "The personal allowance has been frozen since 2021 while living costs have risen sharply, meaning workers are paying more tax in real terms. As wages increase slightly to keep up with inflation, more people are pulled into paying tax or higher rates. Increasing the threshold to £20,000 would put more money into millions of workers' pockets, ease financial pressure, and support low and middle earners during a cost of living crisis."
 Mr Healey made no adjustments to the allowances in the Budget - however he did inform ITV viewers that potentially 'bigger changes' were on the horizon. On his ITV programme, personal finance expert Martin Lewis read out a question from viewer Michael: "Will the Chancellor be honest and admit he's raising taxes on working people by stealth by continuing the freeze on tax thresholds? He is being totally disingenuous."
 Martin asked: "When will you raise tax thresholds?" Mr Healey said: "Well, our promise was not to raise rates across the board and this was a budget unlike in some previous years where I rejected the idea of broad-based tax rises because it isn't just businesses, it's individuals and households that are under pressure.
 "So where I could avoid that, I decided I should do that. And it was a budget, if you step back, that was designed to take action where we could just to help take a bit of pressure off people, give people a bit of breathing space, which we've done, especially on energy. And it was a budget also designed to try and do that a bit for business.
 "So where I could avoid that, I decided I should do that. If you step back, that was designed to take action where we could just to help take a bit of pressure off people, give people a bit of breathing space, which we've done, especially on energy. And it was a budget also designed to try and do that a bit for business."
 However, Martin challenged the claim regarding working people's taxes, arguing that fiscal drag was doing precisely that: "Forgive me, this specific question. You said in the speech yesterday, we are not raising taxes on working people. Well, by all definitions, the fiscal drag, the freezing of the tax thresholds is the biggest tax that has ever been raised in recent history. You accept you are while you're not raising tax rates, you are increasing taxes."
 Mr Healey said: "In truth, it is part of any government's revenue and judgments about thresholds as well as rates are part of the judgments that have to be taken, and the plans for the thresholds have been set for the next few years. And I took the decision in this budget that I wouldn't touch those and I would do what I can where I could to help people. And then make some bigger changes for the long term. Because fundamentally we've got parts of our system that needs fixing."
 Fiscal drag takes effect when the government holds tax thresholds steady while inflation and nominal wages climb. Rather than openly increasing tax rates, the Treasury collects greater revenue as a growing proportion of workers' earnings exceeds the frozen boundaries.
 According to the most recent HMRC figures, there are 31.4 million basic-rate taxpayers across the country — representing a 15% increase in the number of people paying income tax at 20% since tax bands were frozen at 2021 levels.
 Some 7.7 million individuals are expected to pay the higher rate this year — a rise of a million compared to two years ago. A further 1.3 million people are forecast to pay the 45% additional rate — considerably more than the 263,000 people who were subject to it in 2010-11 when it was first introduced.
 Had the threshold risen in line with inflation, it would sit at approximately £16,072 next year and £17,380 by 2029-30, according to analysis by AJ Bell. Were Burnham to opt for raising the personal allowance to £16,000, it would carry a price tag of around £35bn, the investment platform noted.
 Lifting the allowance by just £100 would cost roughly £1bn per year. To view and back the petition, click here.
